{{Short description|Set-theoretic concept}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[set theory]] and [[model theory]], a '''stationary set''' is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] that is not too small in the sense that it intersects all [[club set]]s and is analogous to a set of non-zero measure in [[measure theory]]. There are at least three closely related notions of stationary set, depending on whether one is looking at subsets of an [[Ordinal number|ordinal]], or [[subset]]s of something of given [[cardinality]], or a [[powerset]].

==Classical notion==
If <math>\kappa</math> is a [[cardinal number|cardinal]] of [[uncountable]] [[cofinality]], <math>S \subseteq \kappa,</math> and <math>S</math> [[Intersection (set theory)|intersects]] every [[club set]] in <math>\kappa,</math> then <math>S</math> is called a '''stationary set'''.<ref name=Jech91>Jech (2003) p.91</ref>  If a set is not stationary, then it is called a '''thin set'''. This notion should not be confused with the notion of a [[Thin set (Serre)|thin set in number theory]].

If <math>S</math> is a stationary set and <math>C</math> is a club set, then their intersection <math>S \cap C</math> is also stationary. This is because if <math>D</math> is any club set, then <math>C \cap D</math> is a club set, thus <math>(S \cap C) \cap D = S \cap (C  \cap D)</math> is nonempty. Therefore, <math>(S \cap C)</math> must be stationary.

''See also'': [[Fodor's lemma]]

The restriction to uncountable cofinality is in order to avoid trivialities: Suppose <math>\kappa</math> has countable cofinality. Then <math>S \subseteq \kappa</math> is stationary in <math>\kappa</math> if and only if <math>\kappa\setminus S</math> is bounded in <math>\kappa</math>. In particular, if the cofinality of <math>\kappa</math> is <math>\omega=\aleph_0</math>, then any two stationary subsets of <math>\kappa</math> have stationary intersection.

This is no longer the case if the cofinality of <math>\kappa</math> is uncountable. In fact, suppose <math>\kappa</math> is moreover [[regular cardinal|regular]] and <math>S \subseteq \kappa</math> is stationary. Then <math>S</math> can be partitioned into <math>\kappa</math> many disjoint stationary sets. This result is due to [[Robert M. Solovay|Solovay]]. If <math>\kappa</math> is a [[successor cardinal]], this result is due to [[Stanislaw Ulam|Ulam]] and is easily shown by means of what is called an '''Ulam matrix'''.

[[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|H. Friedman]] has shown that for every countable successor ordinal <math>\beta</math>, every stationary subset of <math>\omega_1</math> contains a [[Club_set#Formal_definition|closed]] subset of order type <math>\beta</math>.

==Jech's notion==
There is also a notion of stationary subset of <math>[X]^\lambda</math>, for <math>\lambda</math> a cardinal and <math>X</math> a set such that <math>|X|\ge\lambda</math>, where <math>[X]^\lambda</math> is the set of subsets of <math>X</math> of cardinality <math>\lambda</math>: <math>[X]^\lambda=\{Y\subseteq X:|Y|=\lambda\}</math>. This notion is due to [[Thomas Jech]]. As before, <math>S\subseteq[X]^\lambda</math> is stationary if and only if it meets every club, where a club subset of <math>[X]^\lambda</math> is a set unbounded under <math>\subseteq</math> and closed under union of chains of length at most <math>\lambda</math>. These notions are in general different, although for <math>X = \omega_1</math> and <math>\lambda = \aleph_0</math> they coincide in the sense that <math>S\subseteq[\omega_1]^\omega</math> is stationary if and only if <math>S\cap\omega_1</math> is stationary in <math>\omega_1</math>.

The appropriate version of Fodor's lemma also holds for this notion.

==Generalized notion==
There is yet a third notion, model theoretic in nature and sometimes referred to as '''generalized''' stationarity. This notion is probably due to [[Menachem Magidor|Magidor]], [[Matthew Foreman|Foreman]] and [[Saharon Shelah|Shelah]] and has also been used prominently by [[W. Hugh Woodin|Woodin]].

Now let <math>X</math> be a nonempty set. A set <math>C\subseteq{\mathcal P}(X)</math> is club (closed and unbounded) if and only if there is a function <math>F:[X]^{<\omega}\to X</math> such that <math>C=\{z:F[[z]^{<\omega}]\subseteq z\}</math>. Here, <math>[y]^{<\omega}</math> is the collection of finite subsets of <math>y</math>.

<math>S\subseteq{\mathcal P}(X)</math> is stationary in <math>{\mathcal P}(X)</math> if and only if it meets every club subset of <math>{\mathcal P}(X)</math>.

To see the connection with model theory, notice that if <math>M</math> is a [[Structure (mathematical logic)|structure]] with [[Universe (mathematics)|universe]] <math>X</math> in a countable language and <math>F</math> is a [[Skolem function]] for <math>M</math>, then a stationary <math>S</math> must contain an elementary substructure of <math>M</math>. In fact, <math>S\subseteq{\mathcal P}(X)</math> is stationary if and only if for any such structure <math>M</math> there is an elementary substructure of <math>M</math> that belongs to <math>S</math>.
